Cleaning names: clutter, titles, credentials and suffixes

Source: vignettes/name-cleaning.Rmd
name-cleaning.Rmd

Names in administrative records rarely arrive clean. A Form 990 Part VII list holds entries like livingston III, Mr. MICHAEL JOHN9, ROBERT NAGLE - SMFA BOARD OF or JANE DOE RN MA TERM ENDED. Before peopleparser can decide which token is the first name and which the surname (see vignette("name-order")), it has to strip everything that is not a name. This article walks through those cleaning steps in the order they run.

The pipeline at a glance 

raw string
  |  sanitize_input()           (parse_names() does this for you;
  |    1. periods -> spaces       parse_name() only with sanitize = TRUE)
  |    2. upper case
  |    3. de_clutter()          drop tenure notes, schedule references, roles
  |    4. prep_name()           drop punctuation and digits, join compounds
  v
tokens (split on spaces)
  |  parse_name()
  |    5. deglue_tokens()       MRWILLIAM -> MR WILLIAM, JRMD -> JR MD
  |    6. positional rules      which titles may be stripped *here*
  |    7. strip prefixes        -> salutation
  |    8. strip suffixes        -> suffix
  |    9. strip status words    -> status
  v
name tokens -> name order and gender
show(c("livingston III,  Mr. MICHAEL JOHN9",
       "ROBERT NAGLE - SMFA BOARD OF",
       "JANE DOE RN MA TERM ENDED"))
#>                                  raw salutation first_name middle_name  last_name suffix status
#> 1 livingston III,  Mr. MICHAEL JOHN9         MR    MICHAEL        JOHN LIVINGSTON    III       
#> 2       ROBERT NAGLE - SMFA BOARD OF                ROBERT                  NAGLE              
#> 3          JANE DOE RN MA TERM ENDED      RN_MA       JANE                    DOE

parse_names() sanitizes the whole vector once. parse_name() assumes its input is already sanitized; pass sanitize = TRUE for raw text.

Step 3: removing clutter with de_clutter()

de_clutter() is a list of regular expressions for noise that shows up after the name: tenure notes, role descriptions, schedule references and date ranges. Most patterns delete everything from the marker to the end of the string.

x <- c("ROBERT NAGLE - SMFA BOARD OF",
       "MARY JONES EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR",
       "JOHN SMITH SEE SCHEDULE O",
       "ANN LEE THROUGH 6/30",
       "MR AND MRS PATRICK VETERS")
data.frame(raw = x, cleaned = de_clutter(x))
#>                             raw         cleaned
#> 1  ROBERT NAGLE - SMFA BOARD OF    ROBERT NAGLE
#> 2 MARY JONES EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR      MARY JONES
#> 3     JOHN SMITH SEE SCHEDULE O     JOHN SMITH 
#> 4          ANN LEE THROUGH 6/30         ANN LEE
#> 5     MR AND MRS PATRICK VETERS  PATRICK VETERS

A few markers are kept as a single word so that they can be reported in the status column later instead of being lost: AS OF ... becomes ASOF, and PAST, FORMER and OUTGOING keep their own word.

de_clutter(c("JOHN SMITH AS OF 6/2019", "ANN LEE FORMER PRESIDENT"))
#> [1] "JOHN SMITH ASOF" "ANN LEE FORMER"

Step 4: normalizing with prep_name()

prep_name() produces the token string the parser works on:

  • periods become spaces, then everything is upper-cased;
  • punctuation is dropped except dashes, which mark compound surnames;
  • digits are dropped and runs of spaces collapse to one;
  • abbreviations that periods split apart are re-joined: PH D to PHD, ED D to EDD, DR PH to DRPH, EX OFFICIO to EXOFFICIO, NON VOTING to NONVOTING, VICE CHAIR to VICECHAIR;
  • surname particles are joined to the following word (VON KAMECKE to VON-KAMECKE, ST CLAIR to ST-CLAIR). Those rules are covered in vignette("name-order").
prep_name(c("livingston III,  Mr. MICHAEL JOHN9",
            "Jane O'Brien-Smith, Ph.D.",
            "THOMAS H VON KAMECKE",
            "SEAN ST CLAIR, VICE CHAIR"))
#> [1] "LIVINGSTON III MR MICHAEL JOHN" "JANE OBRIEN-SMITH PHD"         
#> [3] "THOMAS H VON-KAMECKE"           "SEAN ST-CLAIR VICECHAIR"

The re-joins matter because the pieces are otherwise ambiguous: ED is a given name, VICE is a surname, and ST on its own is in the prefix list.

Step 5: repairing glued tokens

Some records lose the space between a title and a name (MRWILLIAM) or between two credentials (JRMD). parse_name() splits these back apart, but only when census evidence says the pieces are real:

  • A title glued to a given name. MR, MRS, MS, MISS or DR followed by a common census given name is split, unless the whole token is itself a census name. MRWILLIAM splits; DREW and FRANK do not.
  • Two fused credentials. JRMD or MDMPH is split when both parts are known suffixes or credentials. This only applies from the third token on, so a leading given name is never split.
  • A stray initial glued to a surname (CWOOLFOLK). This split is off by default because it cannot be told apart from a given name missing from the census (TSHEPO). Turn it on with split_initials = TRUE when you can check the results another way, for example against the same person in other years.
show(c("MRWILLIAM JONES", "JOHN SMITH JRMD", "DREW CAREY"))
#>               raw salutation first_name middle_name last_name suffix status
#> 1 MRWILLIAM JONES         MR    WILLIAM                 JONES              
#> 2 JOHN SMITH JRMD         MD       JOHN                 SMITH     JR       
#> 3      DREW CAREY                  DREW                 CAREY
parse_name("JOHN CWOOLFOLK", split_initials = TRUE)
#>   salutation first_name middle_name last_name suffix status gender gender_confidence
#> 1                  JOHN           C  WOOLFOLK                    M              99.8

Steps 6-9: stripping titles, credentials, suffixes and status

The removal lists

Three lists of tokens are removed from the name:

  • prx, a few hundred titles, degrees, credentials, ranks, religious-order post-nominals and role words. Whatever is removed goes to salutation.
  • sfx, the generational suffixes JR, JUNIOR, SR, SENIOR, II, III, IV. Removed tokens go to suffix.
  • status words such as RESIGNED, INTERIM, FORMER, PAST, DECEASED and ASOF. Removed tokens go to status.
length(prx)
#> [1] 266
sfx
#> [1] "JR"     "JUNIOR" "SR"     "SENIOR" "II"     "III"    "IV"

A token is removed wherever it sits in the name, not only at the front or the end. When several tokens match, they are all removed and joined with _:

show(c("DR JOHN SMITH MD PHD", "REV JANE DOE JR"))
#>                    raw salutation first_name middle_name last_name suffix status
#> 1 DR JOHN SMITH MD PHD  DR_MD_PHD       JOHN                 SMITH              
#> 2      REV JANE DOE JR        REV       JANE                   DOE     JR

known_titles() gives a label and a type for each token, which helps when you want to keep the credentials rather than throw them away:

titles <- known_titles()
table(titles$type)
#> 
#>            Academic Degree    Civic / Political Title           Fraternal Office 
#>                         57                         15                          5 
#>         Geographic / Other      Honorific / Nobiliary       Military Affiliation 
#>                          1                          1                          9 
#>              Military Rank            Military Status        Organizational Role 
#>                         28                          4                         32 
#>                      Other Personal Name Abbreviation             Personal Title 
#>                          1                          1                          9 
#>    Professional Credential        Religious Honorific            Religious Order 
#>                         84                          1                         22 
#>            Religious Title 
#>                         24
subset(titles, abbr %in% c("RSM", "FACHE", "CFRE", "USNRET"))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   abbr   label                                             type                   
#>   <chr>  <chr>                                             <chr>                  
#> 1 RSM    Religious Sisters of Mercy                        Religious Order        
#> 2 FACHE  Fellow, American College of Healthcare Executives Professional Credential
#> 3 CFRE   Certified Fund Raising Executive                  Professional Credential
#> 4 USNRET U.S. Navy, retired                                Military Status

Tokens that are both a title and a name

The hard part of cleaning is that many titles are also names. BISHOP is a common surname, MA is a surname and a credential, SJ can be initials, and EARL and MAJOR are names as well as titles. Stripping these everywhere would destroy real names, so their removal depends on where they sit.

Rule Tokens (examples) Removed only when
Leading-only titles BISHOP, SHERIFF, CANTOR, DEACON, CAPTAIN, MOTHER, BROTHER, IMAM, MOST, SIR, DAME, CHIEF, COUNCILMAN, CORPORAL, REP, CHAPLAIN they are the first token and two or more tokens follow
Trailing-only titles SJ, CISA, OP, SC, DD, and role words: PRESIDENT, CHAIR, SECRETARY, TREASURER, TRUSTEE, VICECHAIR they sit in the run of known tokens at the end of the name, with at least two tokens before them
Ambiguous credentials MA, BA, AB, NP, PT, DC, ND, RM, PM, APR, … they sit in that trailing run and the run also holds an unambiguous credential
Tenure words TERM, ENDED, JOINED, SINCE, EMERITUS, NONVOTING, … they sit in that trailing run; they go to status 
show(c("BISHOP JOHN SMITH", "JOHN BISHOP",
       "JANE DOE RN MA", "MA LIN",
       "LARRY BLACK SECRETARY",
       "KENT CASHELL TERM ENDED"))
#>                       raw salutation first_name middle_name last_name suffix status
#> 1       BISHOP JOHN SMITH     BISHOP       JOHN                 SMITH              
#> 2             JOHN BISHOP                  JOHN                BISHOP              
#> 3          JANE DOE RN MA      RN_MA       JANE                   DOE              
#> 4                  MA LIN                    MA                   LIN              
#> 5   LARRY BLACK SECRETARY  SECRETARY      LARRY                 BLACK              
#> 6 KENT CASHELL TERM ENDED                  KENT               CASHELL

JOHN BISHOP keeps its surname because BISHOP is not leading. MA LIN keeps MA because it is not in a trailing run with a real credential, while JANE DOE RN MA loses it because RN vouches for it.

The tenure words overlap with de_clutter(). On sanitized input (as above, and always in parse_names()), de_clutter() has already cut TERM ENDED, so status is empty. The tenure-word rule matters for input that skips sanitizing:

parse_name("KENT CASHELL TERM ENDED")[c("first_name", "last_name", "status")]
#>   first_name last_name     status
#> 1       KENT   CASHELL TERM_ENDED

Putting back a name that was stripped

A last safety net catches titles that are also given names. If stripping leaves no first name, and the removed token is a census given name (or JD or ED), the token is restored. Its original position decides its role: a leading token becomes the first name, a trailing one the surname. Ranks and offices (GEN, COL, ADM, SGT, GOV, SEN, HON, REV, SIR) are never restored, although some are rare given names in the 2020 census, so GEN PERRIN keeps GEN as the title.

show(c("EARL FAHNESTOCK", "TOM MAJOR", "GEN PERRIN", "COL RET CLARENCE MAXWELL"))
#>                        raw salutation first_name middle_name  last_name suffix status
#> 1          EARL FAHNESTOCK                  EARL             FAHNESTOCK              
#> 2                TOM MAJOR                   TOM                  MAJOR              
#> 3               GEN PERRIN        GEN                            PERRIN              
#> 4 COL RET CLARENCE MAXWELL        COL   CLARENCE                MAXWELL

Using your own lists

parse_name() and parse_names() take prefixes and suffixes arguments. Extend the defaults rather than replace them, so the built-in credentials are still removed:

x <- "JANE DOE CFRE BOARDCHAIR"
parse_name(x)[c("salutation", "last_name")]
#>        salutation last_name
#> 1 CFRE_BOARDCHAIR       DOE
parse_name(x, prefixes = c(prx, "BOARDCHAIR"))[c("salutation", "last_name")]
#>        salutation last_name
#> 1 CFRE_BOARDCHAIR       DOE

The position rules (leading-only, trailing-only, ambiguous) use fixed internal lists and apply on top of whatever you pass.

Limits

  • The salutation column mixes honorifics (MR), degrees (PHD) and roles (SECRETARY). Use known_titles() to sort them by type.
  • de_clutter() cuts at the first marker it finds, so a surname that is also a marker word in the middle of a name (JOHN FROM SMITH) loses what follows.
  • A credential not in prx survives into the name, often as the last name. The lists were extended from the tokens that leaked on 410,071 Form 990 Part VII names (data-raw/SUFFIX-GAPS-PART7.md), so they fit that source best.
